newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra announces boost for small business.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra announces boost for small business.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Monday announced a batch of new policies to assist small business, including a one-year exemption from unfair-dismissal rules for new employees.
The policy statement, "More Time for Business", was particularly aimed at reducing administrative costs by exempting small business from keeping records to back their fringe benefits tax payments.

The government said it would extend an earlier policy that exempted entrepreneurs from capital gains tax when they sold one small business to buy another. That relief would now cover the sale of shares in a business that would otherwise attract tax on a capital gain.
Howard said the government aimed to change the unfair-dismissal laws so they did not apply to new employees until they had been in the job for a year.
"This will give small business every encouragement to hire new staff confidently, particularly younger, less experienced employees," he said in the policy statement.

However, the Australian Democrats, a minor party in the Senate whose support would be crucial for such a legislative change, said earlier on Monday they opposed a general exclusion of small business from unfair dismissal laws. The current unfair dismissal laws are the result of a deal last year between the Democrats and the Liberal-National government, and Democrats senator Andrew Murray said in a statement the new system should be tried for a year before being changed.
Small business attacked the former Labor government's tougher unfair-dismissal rules, saying they made it too hard to get rid of bad employees.
Howard said in the policy statement the government also aimed to end fringe benefits taxation on car parking that an employer provides on a small business's premises.
Small businesses would be allowed to pay their tax early, if that helped them manage their cash flow.
The government would set up a fund to provide venture capital to small technology firms, Howard said.
The cost of the Small Business Innovation Fund -- A$130 million in its first four years -- would come from an existing research-and-development programme.
